# 1 Chronicles Chapter 11 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 376v–377r

---

**1** All Israel came together to David at Hebron and said, "We are your own flesh and blood! **2** Even when Saul was king, you were the one who actually led Israel's armies. And the LORD your God promised you: 'You will be the shepherd of my people Israel; you will be their ruler.'"

**3** So all the elders of Israel came to David at Hebron. He made a covenant with them there in the LORD's presence, and they anointed him king over Israel, just as the LORD had spoken through Samuel.

**4** David and all Israel then marched to Jerusalem — known then as Jebus — where the Jebusites, the original inhabitants, still lived. **5** The Jebusites taunted David: "You'll never get in here!" But David captured the fortress of Zion, which became known as the City of David. **6** David had said, "Whoever leads the attack against the Jebusites will become my chief commander." Joab son of Zeruiah led the charge, and so he became the chief.

**7** David made the fortress his home, and that is why it is called the City of David. **8** He rebuilt and expanded the city outward from the supporting terraces, while Joab restored the rest of Jerusalem. **9** David grew steadily more powerful, because the LORD of Armies was with him.

**10** Here is the roster of David's elite warriors — the men who, together with all Israel, threw their full strength behind making him king, in fulfillment of the LORD's word concerning Israel.

**11** Jashobeam son of a Hachmonite was chief of the Thirty. He once single-handedly killed three hundred men with his spear.

**12** Next was Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite, one of the three greatest warriors. **13** He was with David at Pas-dammim when the Philistines massed for battle. There was a field full of barley, and the Israelite troops were running from the Philistines. **14** But Eleazar and David took their stand in the middle of that field, defended it, and cut down the Philistines. The LORD gave them a tremendous victory.

**15** On another occasion, three of the Thirty's top leaders came down to David at the cave of Adullam while the Philistine army was camped in the Valley of Rephaim. **16** David was in his stronghold at the time, and a Philistine garrison occupied Bethlehem. **17** David said wistfully, "If only someone could bring me a drink of water from the well by the gate of Bethlehem!" **18** So the three warriors fought their way through the Philistine lines, drew water from the well by the gate of Bethlehem, and carried it back to David. But he refused to drink it. Instead, he poured it out as an offering to the LORD. **19** "God forbid that I should drink this!" he said. "This water is as precious as the blood of these men who risked their lives to get it." So he would not drink it. Such were the feats of the three greatest warriors.

**20** Abishai, Joab's brother, was the leader of another group of three. He once killed three hundred men with his spear and gained a reputation equal to the greatest. **21** He was the most distinguished of this second group and became their commander, though he did not quite rank with the top three.

**22** Benaiah son of Jehoiada was a fearless warrior from Kabzeel who accomplished remarkable feats. He struck down two of Moab's mightiest champions. He also climbed into a pit on a snowy day and killed a lion. **23** He once took on an Egyptian giant — a man seven and a half feet tall — who was armed with a spear as thick as a weaver's beam. Benaiah went at him with nothing but a club, wrenched the spear from the Egyptian's grip, and killed him with it. **24** Such were the exploits of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, which earned him fame among the three greatest warriors. **25** He was more honored than any of the Thirty, though he did not rank with the top three. David appointed him commander of his personal bodyguard.

**26** Other elite warriors included: Asahel, Joab's brother; Elhanan son of Dodo from Bethlehem; **27** Shammoth from Harod; Helez from Pelon; **28** Ira son of Ikkesh from Tekoa; Abiezer from Anathoth; **29** Sibbecai from Hushah; Ilai from Ahoh; **30** Maharai from Netophah; Heled son of Baanah from Netophah; **31** Ithai son of Ribai from Gibeah in Benjamin; Benaiah from Pirathon; **32** Hurai from the ravines of Gaash; Abiel from Arabah; **33** Azmaveth from Baharum; Eliahba from Shaalbon; **34** the sons of Hashem from Gizon; Jonathan son of Shagee from Harar; **35** Ahiam son of Sachar from Harar; Eliphal son of Ur; **36** Hepher from Mecherah; Ahijah from Pelon; **37** Hezro from Carmel; Naarai son of Ezbai; **38** Joel, Nathan's brother; Mibhar son of Hagri; **39** Zelek the Ammonite; Naharai from Beeroth, Joab's armor-bearer; **40** Ira the Ithrite; Gareb the Ithrite; **41** Uriah the Hittite; Zabad son of Ahlai; **42** Adina son of Shiza the Reubenite, a leader among the Reubenites, with thirty men under him; **43** Hanan son of Maacah; Joshaphat the Mithnite; **44** Uzzia from Ashteroth; Shama and Jeiel, sons of Hotham from Aroer; **45** Jediael son of Shimri, and his brother Joha, the Tizite; **46** Eliel the Mahavite; Jeribai and Joshaviah, sons of Elnaam; Ithmah the Moabite; **47** Eliel, Obed, and Jaasiel the Mezobaite.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1-3 — The covenant at Hebron:** Notice what the Chronicler omits — the entire seven-year civil war between David's faction and Saul's surviving son Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 2-4). In the Chronicler's telling, all Israel comes to David immediately and unanimously. The transition is seamless because it is divinely ordained.

**Verse 17-19 — Water as blood:** This story reveals David's character at its finest. Three men risk their lives for a cup of water, and David, overwhelmed by the cost, refuses to treat it as ordinary. He pours it out to God — the only one worthy of receiving what cost human blood to obtain. The verb for "poured out" (*nasakh*) is the technical term for a drink offering.

**Verse 41 — Uriah the Hittite:** A devastating name buried in a list. The Chronicler includes Uriah among David's most loyal warriors — the man David will later betray and arrange to have killed (2 Samuel 11). The list remembers what the narrative will try to suppress.

*— PNEUMA*
